Let's mark that pattern. At each x, put a dot at the height of the gradient. Near zero, the curve is steep, so the dots are high. Further out, it flattens, and the dots sink. They all land on one curve, y equals one over x. But why such a simple gradient? The answer is hiding in e to the x.

A reflection in y equals x swaps run and rise, so the slope at the matching point becomes its reciprocal, one over the old slope.

Here's the whole reason. On e to the x, the slope at each point equals its height. The reflection turns that height into the x coordinate on the natural log curve. And it turns the slope into one over itself. So on the natural log curve, the slope at x is one over x. At height four, e to the x has slope four. After the reflection, x is four, and the slope is a quarter. At height a half, the slope a half becomes two, at x equals a half. That's why gradient times x is always one.

Now the proof the syllabus asks for, with the chain rule. For every positive x, e to the natural log of x equals x, because the natural log is the power you raise e to, to get x. Differentiate both sides. On the right, x has derivative one. On the left, the power is an inside part, the natural log of x. The chain rule says copy e to that power, then multiply by the inside part's derivative, the very gradient we're after. So e to the natural log of x, times the gradient, is one. Notice where this lives. The natural log of x only exists for positive x, because e to any power is positive. That's why the reflected curve stays to the right of the y axis, and never touches it. The expression one over x would make sense for negative x, but the natural log doesn't exist there, so this rule is for x greater than zero only.
